newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says 100,000 Rwandan Hutus heading home.
newsitem.headline: UN says 100,000 Rwandan Hutus heading home.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said on Friday that more than 100,000 Rwandan Hutus fleeing Tutsi rebels in east Zaire were heading back to their own country in one of the largest homeward refugee movements in its history.

UNHCR spokesman Fernando del Mundo told Reuters that some 10,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees crossed into Rwanda earlier on Friday and 100,000 more were on the way home more than two years after their exodus into Zaire.
"They are all heading towards Rwanda. We are gearing up to receive these people in Rwanda. We expect at least 100,000 Rwandan refugees in Rwanda by the end of the day," he said.
This would be one of the the largest, swiftest homeward movements in the history of UNHCR, other officials said.
Tens of thousands of local Zaireans displaced by the fighting further west in Sake region northwest of Goma were also heading for Goma town, Del Mundo said.
The UNHCR's regional spokesman based in Rwanda, Paul Stromberg, said this could be the beginning of the end to a two-year-old deadlock over Africa's worst refugee crisis.
"We hope this is finally the breakthrough. The momentum now is in the direction of a return," Stromberg told British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) television.
The refugees were among one million Hutus who fled to east Zaire with the entire former extremist Hutu government and its army after 1994's genocide of Tutsis.
Many among them killed or watched others kill and fear reprisals in Rwanda where a Tutsi-dominated army now holds sway.

The refugees were costing the world $1 million a day in aid and many Western diplomats privately advocated a forced return home to break the deadlock, despite security concerns in Rwanda where 90,000 Hutus accused of complicity in genocide are held in crowded jails.
Many Hutus have also died in apparent reprisal attacks, although the Kigali government has condemned such action.

Rwanda is Africa's most densely-populated country and aid officials say it is ill-equipped to settle large numbers of returnees. Houses of many Hutu refugees have been occupied by diaspora Tutsis, up to 800,000 of whom recently returned home -- nearly a one-to-one replacement of the genocide dead.
Extremist Hutu militamen who played a key role in the genocide held tremendous sway over the refugees and prevented their return with tales of terror and death in Rwanda.
Del Mundo said many of the returnees in Gisenyi were women and children, suggesting that the hold of militiamen may finally be broken.

He said the refugees who had crossed into Rwanda were in good shape and would be moved to a camp near the frontier which previously sheltered Zairean ethnic Tutsis fleeing the troubled Masisi region west of Goma.

The arrivals were being screened by soldiers of Rwanda's army at no-man's land between the two borders. UNHCR had no reports of arrests so far at the border. Rwanda's Tutsi-led government has repeatedly said that refugees who took part in the slaughters will not be immune from arrest.
In Rome, the U.N.'s World Food Programme (WFP) said it hoped the exodus meant a possible breakthrough in the crisis.

"This is the break we've been hoping for. While it may not effect all the (refugee) population in terms of everybody coming back it could be a major breakthrough if they cross into Rwanda," WFP spokesman Trevor Rowe told Reuters during a world food summit.
